Leczyca Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Łęczyca, Poland

Demolished. Łęczyca, granted town rights before 1267 and once capital of its own principality, saw Jewish settlement from the 15th century, becoming central Poland's largest Jewish community by the mid-18th century; by the late 19th century, 3,639 Jews (45%) lived there. Notable rabbis include Icchak Chaim Auerbach and Meir ben Jehiel Weiser (the Malbim), whose disputes with community factions led opponents and supporters to be buried in separate old and new sections of this cemetery. Established probably in the second half of the 15th century and expanded in the 1830s, the site held the Auerbach family ohel until WWII, housing Rabbi Chaim Auerbach and his son, sofer-rabbi Izaak Chaim Auerbach. In 1939, Łęczyca's starost ordered tombstones removed for paving Belwederska Street toward the railway station; postwar authorities designated the grounds for housing. A 1942 ghetto liquidation deported 2,000 residents to Chełmno. Three preserved tombstones (oldest 1820) are held at the Łęczyca Regional Museum; Isaac Frenkel's 1953 Tel Aviv-published 'Sefer Linshits' (Memorial Book of Łęczyca) documents the cemetery further.
